Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 40, verses 2–3:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, Severe in punishment, Owner of bounty. There is no deity except Him﴾

He used the conjunction (waw) between the first two names but not between the latter ones. Al-Suhayli said: The conjunction between the first two names is good only because they are attributes of actions (sifat al-af'al), and His action is directed toward others, not toward Himself. So the conjunction was used to mark a sound distinction between the two meanings, and to place them in the position of two sentences, because He intends to alert His servants that He does this and does that, so that they may hope in Him and aspire to Him. Then he said: ﴿Severe in punishment﴾ without a waw, because severity returns to the meaning of strength and power, and that is a meaning outside the attributes of actions. So it stands in the position of His saying: ﴿the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾. Likewise His saying: ﴿Owner of bounty﴾, because the word dhu (possessor) is an expression for His essence. This is his answer, and as you see it is neither satisfying nor sufficient, for the severity of His punishment is an attribute of actions, and His bounty is an attribute of actions.

The word (dhu) in it does not remove it from being an attribute of action, as in His saying: ﴿Mighty, Possessor of retribution﴾. Rather, describing Him with (ghafir) and (qabil) is more indicative of the essence than describing Him with (dhu), because dhu means "possessor" (sahib). Thus a derived descriptive attribute is more indicative of the essence than one formed with it.

So his answer did not satisfy; rather it added another question to the question.

Know that this sentence contains six names, each two of which form a group. He began with (al-Aziz al-Alim), which are two absolute names and attributes of His essence, and they are free of conjunction. Then he mentioned after them two names of His attributes of action and placed the conjunction between them. Then he mentioned two other names after them and left them free of the conjunction.

As for the first two, they are free of the conjunction because they are two singular attributes applying to the name of God, and they are mutually entailing, so leaving them free of conjunction is the basic form, and it agrees with what the Glorious Book shows of this, such as: the Mighty, the All-Knowing; the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing; the Forgiving, the Merciful.

As for ﴿The Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance﴾, the conjunction was placed between them because they are in the meaning of sentences, and although they are singular in wording, they convey the meaning "He forgives sin and accepts repentance."

That is, this is His condition and His attribute at all times. He brought the name that indicates that this is His attribute and description, containing the meaning of an action that indicates He never ceases doing that. So one was conjoined to the other in the manner of conjoining sentences to one another, and this is not so for the first two names.

Since the action is not considered in ﴿Severe in punishment, Owner of bounty﴾, for it is not good for an action to occur in them, and there is nothing in the word ﴿dhu﴾ from which an action is derived that runs in the manner of the singular names in every respect, and one was not conjoined to the other just as it was not conjoined in "the Mighty, the All-Knowing." So reflect on it, for it is clear.

Addendum: Consider how the description "Severe in punishment" falls between an attribute of mercy before it and an attribute of mercy after it. Before it is ﴿The Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance﴾, and after it is ﴿Owner of bounty﴾.

In this there is confirmation of, and evidence for, the authentic hadith in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed Allah wrote a book which is deposited with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy overcomes My anger."

Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

And in another wording: "My mercy precedes My anger."

Here the attribute of mercy has preceded and prevailed.

Consider how He opened the verse with His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾, and "revelation" (tanzil) necessarily implies the loftiness of the one from whom it is sent down. The Arabs, by their language, and indeed other sound-natured peoples, understand nothing but that.

He has informed that the revelation of the Book is from Him, and this indicates two things:

The first is His exaltedness above His creation.

The second is that He is the speaker of the Book sent down from Him, not another, for He informed that it is from Him, and this requires that it be from Him as speech just as it is from Him as revelation.

For if another were the speaker of it, the Book would be from that other, since speech is attributed to the one who speaks it. Similar to this is ﴿But the word from Me is established﴾, and similar is ﴿Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord﴾, and similar is ﴿A revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy﴾.

So hold fast to the particle (min, "from") in these places, for it cuts off the arguments of the Mu'tazila factions and the Jahmiyya.

And consider how He said: ﴿A revelation from﴾ and did not say "its revelation"?

Thus the verse includes affirmation of His exaltedness, His place, and the establishment of the messengership.

Then He said: ﴿the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾. These two names include the attributes of power and knowledge, the creation of human actions, and the origination of all that is other than God, because power is the power of God, as Ahmad ibn Hanbal said; so it includes affirmation of divine decree (qadar). Also, His might prevents anything in His dominion that He does not will, or that He wills not to occur; so His might nullifies that.

Likewise, the perfection of His power requires that He be the creator of everything, and that negates that there be in the world anything eternal to which His creation is not related, for the perfection of His power and might nullifies that.

Then He said: ﴿The Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance﴾. Sin is opposing His law and command, so these two names include affirmation of His law, His kindness and His grace.

Then He said: ﴿Severe in punishment﴾, and this is His recompense for the sinners, and ﴿Owner of bounty﴾ is His recompense for the good-doers; so it includes reward and punishment.

Then He said: ﴿There is no deity except Him. To Him is the final return﴾, so this includes monotheism (tawhid) and the return (ma'ad).

Thus the two verses include affirmation of the attribute of height, speech, power, knowledge, qadar, the origination of the world, reward and punishment, monotheism and the return; and the revelation of the Book from Him upon the tongue of His Messenger includes messengership and prophethood.

These are ten foundations of Islam and faith, displayed to your hearing in this great verse. But:

A bride is escorted to a blind, paralyzed man.

Has it ever occurred to you that this verse contains these sciences and knowledge, despite how often you recite it and hear it, and likewise all the verses of the Qur'an?

How grievous a regret, and how great a loss for one who spends his life seeking knowledge, then leaves this world without having understood the realities of the Qur'an, or having his heart touched by its secrets and meanings. And God is the one sought for help.

(Benefit)

He, glory be to Him, couples the vastness of knowledge with mercy, just as He couples knowledge with forbearance (hilm). From the first is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾.

And from the second: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾.

So no thing has been coupled with another better than forbearance with knowledge, and mercy with knowledge.

The bearers of the Throne are four: two of them say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; to You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge," and two of them say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; to You be praise for Your pardon after Your power." So the pairing of pardon with power is like the pairing of forbearance and mercy with knowledge, because pardon is only fitting when one has power, and likewise forbearance and mercy are only fitting when accompanied by knowledge.

(Section)

Among the supplications of the angels for the believers is their saying: ﴿And protect them from evil deeds. And whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You have certainly had mercy on him﴾ [Ghafir: 9].

This includes a request for their protection from the evil deeds and their consequences that harm the one who commits them. Whenever He protects them from doing evil, He protects them from the punishment for evil. Although His words ﴿and whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day, You have certainly had mercy on him﴾ appear more clearly in reference to the consequences of deeds, the protection requested on that Day is evident.

If it is said: They asked Him to protect them from the punishment of Hellfire, and this is the protection from evil consequences. This indicates that what is meant by the evil deeds from which they asked protection is the evil actions themselves, so what the angels asked for is the counterpart of what the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge from.

This is not contradicted by His words "that Day," because what is sought is protection from the evils of deeds on that Day, and those are evils in themselves.

It is said: The protection from evil deeds is of two kinds.

The first: protection from doing them through success (tawfiq), so that they do not proceed from him.

The second: protection from their punishment through forgiveness, so that he is not punished for them. The verse thus includes a request for both matters, and the temporal phrase qualifies the conditional clause, not the imperative clause.

Reflect on what this report about the angels contains of their praise for faith, righteous deeds, and kindness toward the believers by seeking forgiveness for them. Before their request for forgiveness, they made a means of approach to God through the vastness of His knowledge and the vastness of His mercy. The vastness of His knowledge includes His knowledge of their sins and their causes, their weakness in preserving themselves from error, the domination of their enemy, their own souls, their desires and natures, and what the world and its adornments have made attractive to them; His knowledge of them when He created them from the earth, and when they were embryos in their mothers' wombs; His foreknowledge that they must disobey Him; and that He loves pardon and forgiveness; and other aspects of His vast knowledge which no one besides Him encompasses.

The vastness of His mercy includes that none of the believers who affirm His oneness and love Him will perish, for He is of vast mercy and excludes from the circle of His mercy none but the wretched. And none is more wretched than one whom His mercy, which encompasses all things, does not embrace. Then they asked Him to forgive those who repent and follow His path, which is His straight way that leads to Him, namely knowledge of Him, love of Him, and obedience to Him. So they repent from what He dislikes and follow the way He loves. Then they asked Him to protect them from the punishment of Hellfire, and to admit them, and the believers among their forefathers, their descendants, and their spouses, into the Gardens of Eden which He promised them. Although He does not break His promise, He promised them these by means (asbab), and among these means is the angels' supplication for them that He admit them into these gardens by His mercy, which is among the things by which He enabled them to do their deeds, and by which He appointed angels to supplicate for them.

Then God informed about His angels that they said, following this supplication: ﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [Ghafir: 8].

That is: the source, cause, and ultimate purpose of all this proceeds from the perfection of Your power and the perfection of Your knowledge, for might is the perfection of power and wisdom is the perfection of knowledge. By these two attributes He, glorified and exalted, decrees what He wills, commands and forbids, rewards and punishes. These two attributes are thus the source of creation and command.

The point is that the punishments for evil deeds are of various kinds: legislated punishments (shar'iyyah) and decreed punishments (qadariyyah), which may be in the heart, in the body, or in both; punishments in the intermediate realm (barzakh) after death; and punishments on the day the bodies are returned. Sin never fails to bring some punishment, but because of the servant's ignorance he does not perceive what punishment it contains, for he is like one intoxicated, drugged, or asleep, who feels no pain. The consequences of sins following upon them is like the burning following fire, the breaking following fragility, drowning following water, the corruption of the body following poisons, and diseases following their causes. Harm may coincide with the sin or may be delayed after it, either briefly or for a period, just as a disease may be delayed after its cause rather than coinciding with it. Very often the servant errs in this matter: he commits a sin and sees no effect immediately after it, and does not realize that it is working on him gradually, step by step, just as poisons and harmful things work precisely. If the servant does not remedy himself with medicines, purgation, and regimen, he is headed for destruction. This is the case with a single sin he has not remedied by what removes its effect; how much more so with sin upon sin, every day and every hour? And God is the one sought for help.

This is the case with a single sin he has not remedied by what removes its effect; how much more so with sin upon sin, every day and every hour? And God is the one sought for help.

(Section heading)
Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said in his book al-Milal wa'l-Nihal: As for the one who thinks that the dead will be made alive in his grave before the Day of Resurrection, he is mistaken, for the verses we have cited prevent this, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice"﴾
and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life again﴾
He said: If the dead were to be alive in his grave, then He, exalted is He, would have made us die three times and given us life three times, and this is false and contrary to the Qur'an, except for one whom Allah, exalted is He, made alive as a sign for one of the prophets, like those who left their homes, being thousands, fearing death, so Allah said to them, "Die," then He brought them back to life; and like the one who passed by a town that was fallen upon its roofs; and whom a text specifies. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾
So it is established by the text of the Qur'an that the souls of all those we have mentioned do not return to their bodies except until the appointed term, which is the Day of Resurrection. Likewise, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that on the night he was taken on the Night Journey, at the lowest heaven, he saw the souls: on the right of Adam were the souls of the people of happiness, and on his left the souls of the people of wretchedness. He also informed, on the Day of Badr, when he addressed the dead, that they had heard his words before they had graves, and he did not object to the Companions' saying that they had become putrid; yet he knew that they were hearing his words nonetheless. So it is established without doubt that the address and the hearing were only to their souls. As for the body, it has no sensation, and Allah, exalted is He, has said, ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾
So He negated hearing from those in the graves, which are the bodies, without doubt. And no Muslim doubts that the hearing which Allah, mighty and majestic, negated is other than the hearing which the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed.
He said: No authentic report has ever come from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, that the souls of the dead are returned to their bodies at the time of questioning; and if that were established from him, we would say so. He said: Only Manhal ibn Amr alone transmitted this addition, that the souls are returned to their bodies in the graves; and he is not strong; Shu'bah and others abandoned him; and al-Mughirah ibn Miqsam al-Dabbi, who was one of the imams, said of him: Manhal ibn Amr's testimony was never permitted in Islam, as has been transmitted; and the other established reports are contrary to that.
He said: What we have said is also what is established from the Companions.
Then he mentioned, by the route of Ibn Uyaynah from Mansur ibn Safiyyah from his mother Safiyyah bint Shaybah, who said: Ibn Umar entered the mosque and saw Ibn al-Zubayr thrown down before he was buried. It was said to him, "This is Asma bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq." So Ibn Umar turned to her, consoled her, and said: "These bodies are nothing, and the souls are with Allah." Then his mother said: "What prevents me, when the head of Yahya ibn Zakariyya was presented as a gift to a prostitute of the prostitutes of the Children of Israel?"

(I say) What Abu Muhammad mentioned contains truth and falsehood. As for his saying, "Whoever thinks the dead will be made alive in his grave is mistaken," this is ambiguous. If he means by it the life known in this world, in which the soul manages and directs the body and the person needs food, drink and clothing, then this is mistaken as he said, and sense and reason refute it just as the text refutes it.
But if he means by it another life, other than this life, rather the soul is returned to him by a return other than the usual return in this world, so that he may be questioned and tested in his grave, then this is true and denying it is mistaken, and the clear authentic text indicates it, namely his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "It is returned into his body." We will mention the answer to his weakening of the hadith, God willing.
As for his use of the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice"﴾ it does not negate this temporary return of the soul into the body, just as the slain man of the Children of Israel whom Allah brought to life after he was killed and then caused to die again did not have that temporary life for the purpose of questioning considered lasting; for he was alive for a moment, such that he said, "So-and-so killed me," then he fell dead.
Moreover, his saying, "then its soul is returned into its body," does not indicate a stable life; it only indicates a return of it to the body, and the soul remained attached to its body even when it decayed and was torn apart.
The secret of this is that the soul has five kinds of attachment to the body, differing in their rulings:
(First) its attachment to it in the mother's womb as a fetus.
(Second) its attachment to it after its emergence onto the face of the earth.
(Third) its attachment to it in the state of sleep; so it has attachment to it from one aspect and separation from another.
(Fourth) its attachment to it in the barzakh; for although it has separated from it and become detached from it, it has not separated from it with a complete separation such that it no longer has any regard for it at all. We have mentioned at the beginning of this answer, from the hadiths and reports, what indicates its return to it at the time of the greeting of the Muslim. This return is a specific return which does not necessitate the life of the body before the Day of Resurrection.
(Fifth) its attachment to it on the day the bodies are raised, which is the most complete kind of its attachment to the body, and there is no comparison between the earlier kinds of attachment and it, for it is an attachment with which the body accepts neither death, nor sleep, nor decay.
As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾
His keeping those upon whom He has decreed death does not contradict their return to their dead bodies at some time, as a temporary return which does not necessitate for them the life known in this world.
And since the sleeper's soul is in his body while he is alive, and his life is not the life of one who is awake, for sleep is the twin of death, likewise the dead person, when his soul is returned to his body, his state is intermediate between the living and the dead whose soul has not returned to his body, like the state of the sleeper, which is intermediate between the living and the dead. Reflect on this, for it will dispel from you many difficulties.
As for the Prophet's, peace and blessings be upon him, report about seeing the prophets on the night he was taken on the Night Journey, some people of hadith claimed that what he saw were their figures and their souls, and he said: "They are alive with their Lord," and he saw Ibrahim leaning his back against the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), and he saw Musa standing in his grave praying, and when he saw the prophets he described them as figures: he saw Musa as a tall, lean, brown man, as if he were one of the men of Shanu'ah; and he saw Isa with his head dripping, as if he had just come out of a bathhouse. And he saw Ibrahim and likened him to himself.
Others disputed this and said: That vision was only of their souls, not their bodies, and the bodies are definitely in the earth; they will only be raised on the day the bodies are raised, and they were not raised before that, for if they had been raised before that, the earth would have split open over them before the Day of Resurrection, and they would have tasted death at the blast of the Trumpet, and this would be a third death, and this is definitely false. And if the bodies had been raised from the graves, Allah would not have returned them to them but they would have been in Paradise. It is authentically reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Allah has forbidden Paradise to the prophets until he enters it himself, and he is the first to ask for the opening of the gate of Paradise, and he is the first whom the earth splits open for, absolutely, none before him having been split open for."
It is known by necessity that his body, peace and blessings be upon him, is fresh in the earth, and the Companions asked him: "How will our prayers be presented to you when you have decayed?" He said: "Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets."
Had his body not been in his tomb, he would not have answered with this answer.
It is also authentically reported from him that Allah has appointed angels over his grave who convey to him the greetings of his community.
And it is authentically reported from him that he went out between Abu Bakr and Umar and said: "Thus shall we be raised."
This is with certainty that his noble soul is in the Highest Companionship, in the highest of the 'Illiyyun, together with the souls of the prophets.
And it is authentically reported from him that he saw Musa standing praying in his grave on the night of the Night Journey, and he saw him in the sixth or seventh heaven. So the soul was there, and it has connection to the body in the grave and oversight over it and attachment to it, such that it prays in its grave and returns the greeting of whoever greets it, while the soul is in the Highest Companionship.
There is no contradiction between the two matters, for the affairs of souls differ from the affairs of bodies. You find two souls that are alike and compatible in the utmost closeness and proximity, even if between them is the distance of the two easts; and you find two souls that are repellent and hostile with the utmost distance between them, even if their bodies are adjacent and touching.
The descent, ascent, nearness and distance of the soul are not of the same kind as those of the body, for it ascends above the heavens and then descends to the earth in the interval between its being taken and the placing of the dead in his grave, which is a brief time in which a body cannot ascend and descend. Likewise its ascent and return to the body during sleep and waking. Some have likened it to the sun and its ray: it is in the sky while its ray is on the earth. Our Shaykh said: This is not an exact parallel, for the sun itself does not descend from the sky, and the ray on the earth is not the sun nor its attribute, but an accident produced by the sun and the opposing body; whereas the soul itself ascends and descends.
As for the Companions' saying to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, regarding the slain of Badr: "How do you address people who have become putrid?", despite his informing them that they hear his speech, this does not negate the return of their souls to their bodies at that time, a return by which they heard his address, while the bodies had become putrid. So the address was to the souls attached to those bodies which had decayed.
As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You cannot make those in the graves hear﴾
the context of the verse indicates that what is meant is that the dead disbeliever whose heart is dead cannot be made to hear in a way that benefits him, just as those in the graves cannot be made to hear in a way that benefits them. He, glorified is He, did not intend that the people of the graves hear nothing at all. How could that be, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that they hear the sound of the sandals of those who follow the funeral?
And he informed that the slain of Badr heard his speech and address, and he prescribed greeting them with the form of address to one present who hears; and he informed that whoever greets his believing brother, he returns the greeting.
This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating﴾
It may be said: the negation of making the deaf hear together with the negation of making the dead hear indicates that the intended meaning is the lack of capacity of each of them for hearing, and that since the hearts of these people were dead and deaf, making them hear was impossible, in the position of addressing the dead and the deaf. This is true. But it does not negate making the souls hear after death a hearing of rebuke and reproach through their attachment to the bodies at some time. This is other than the negated hearing; and Allah knows best. The real meaning is that you cannot make hear whom Allah has not willed to make hear; you are only a warner, i.e., Allah has given you capacity only for the warning with which He has charged you, not for making hear those whom Allah has not willed to make hear.
As for his saying that the hadith is not authentic because Manhal ibn Amr alone transmitted it and he is not strong, this is one of his rash judgments, may Allah have mercy on him. The hadith is authentic beyond doubt, and it was transmitted from al-Bara ibn Azib by a group other than Zadhan, among them Adi ibn Thabit, Muhammad ibn Uqbah, and Mujahid.
(He said) The memorizer Abu Abdullah ibn Mandah in his book al-Ruh wa'l-Nafs informed us: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub ibn Yusuf related to us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Saffar related to us, Abu'l-Nadr Hashim ibn al-Qasim informed us, Isa ibn al-Musayyib related to us from Adi ibn Thabit from al-Bara ibn Azib, who said: We went out with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, in the funeral of a man of the Ansar. We reached the grave and it had not yet been dug into a niche (lahd), so we sat down, and he sat as if birds were upon our heads and as if there were splinters of rock on our shoulders. He was silent for a while, and silence is called "iram." When he raised his head he said:
"Indeed, when the believer is in the front of the Hereafter and the back of this world, the Angel of Death comes to him, and angels descend upon him from heaven with a shroud from Paradise and perfume from Paradise, and they sit as far as the eye can see. The Angel of Death comes and sits at his head and says: 'Come out, O tranquil soul, come out to the mercy of Allah and His pleasure.' His soul then flows out like a drop flowing from a waterskin. When his soul has departed, every creature between heaven and earth prays for him except the two jinn and humans. Then he is taken up to heaven, and the heaven's gates are opened for him, and those near to it escort him to the second heaven, the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, and the seventh, to the Throne, with those nearest to each heaven accompanying him. When he reaches the Throne, his book is written in 'Illiyyun, and the Lord, mighty and majestic, says: 'Return My servant to his resting place, for I have promised him that I created them from it, and into it I return them, and from it I bring them out once more.' So he is returned to his resting place, and Munkar and Nakir come to him, stirring up the earth with their fangs and searching the earth with their hair. They seat him, then it is said to him: 'O such-and-such, who is your Lord?' He says: 'My Lord is Allah.' They say: 'You have spoken truly.' Then it is said to him: 'What is your religion?' He says: 'My religion is Islam.' They say: 'You have spoken truly.' Then it is said to him: 'Who is your Prophet?' He says: 'Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' They say: 'You have spoken truly.' Then his grave is widened as far as the eye can see, and there comes to him a man of beautiful face, sweet scent, and fine clothing, who says: 'May Allah reward you with good. By Allah, I have known that you were quick in obedience to Allah and slow in disobedience to Allah.' He says: 'And may you be rewarded with good. Who are you?' He says: 'I am your righteous deed.' Then a door to Paradise is opened for him, and he looks at his place and station in it until the Hour is established.

And when the disbeliever is in the back of this world and the front of the Hereafter, and the Angel of Death comes to him, angels descend upon him from heaven with a shroud of Fire and perfume of Fire." He said: "They sit as far as the eye can see. An angel comes and sits at his head and says: 'Come out, O evil soul, come out to the wrath and anger of Allah.' His soul is scattered in his body, for it dislikes to come out because of what it sees and witnesses. He draws it out as a skewer is drawn out of wet wool. When his soul has departed, everything between heaven and earth curses him except the two jinn and humans. Then he is taken up to heaven, but it is refused him. The Lord, mighty and majestic, says: 'Return My servant to his resting place, for I have promised them that I created them from it, and into it I return them, and from it I bring them out once more.' So his soul is returned to his resting place, and Munkar and Nakir come to him, stirring up the earth with their fangs and searching the earth with their hair; their voices are like thundering crashes, and their eyes like flashing lightning. They seat him and say: 'O such-and-such, who is your Lord?' He says: 'I do not know.' A voice calls from the side of the grave: 'You did not know!' They strike him with an iron mace which, if all between the two horizons gathered to lift it, they could not lift it. And his grave is constricted upon him until his ribs interlock. A man of ugly face, foul clothing, and stinking smell comes to him and says: 'May Allah reward you with evil. By Allah, I have known that you were slow in obedience to Allah and quick in disobedience to Allah.' He says: 'Who are you?' He says: 'I am your evil deed.' Then a door to the Fire is opened for him, and he looks at his place in it until the Hour is established."

Imam Ahmad, Mahmud ibn Abi Ghaylan and others transmitted it from Abu'l-Nadr. In it is that the souls are returned to the grave, and that the two angels seat the dead person and question him.

(Then) Ibn Mandah cited it by the route of Muhammad ibn Salamah from Khusayf al-Jazari from Mujahid from al-Bara ibn Azib, who said: We were in the funeral of a man of the Ansar, with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, with us. We reached the grave and it had not been dug into a niche, and the bier was set down, and the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, sat and said:

The soul of the believer, when he is dying, the Angel of Death comes to him in the best of forms and with the sweetest scent, and sits beside him to take his soul. Two angels come to him with embalming spices from Paradise and a shroud from Paradise, and they stand at a distance from him. The Angel of Death draws out his soul from his body gently, like a drop of sweat. When it reaches the Angel of Death, the two angels hasten to take it from him. They wrap it in the embalming spices of Paradise and shroud it in the shroud of Paradise. Then they ascend with it to Paradise. The gates of heaven are opened for it, and the angels rejoice at it and say: "For whom is this good soul, for which the gates of heaven have been opened?" It is called by the best names it was called by in the world, and it is said: "This is the soul of so-and-so." When it ascends to heaven, the angels nearest to God in each heaven escort it, until it is placed before God, at the Throne. Then the deeds of that person are brought out from 'Illiyyin, and Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the angels who are nearest to Him: "Bear witness that I have forgiven the doer of this deed." Then his book is sealed and returned to 'Illiyyin. Allah, mighty and majestic, says: "Return the soul of My servant to the earth, for I have promised them that I will return them to it." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once more﴾.

When the believer is placed in his grave, a door is opened for him at his feet toward Paradise, and it is said to him: "Look at what Allah has prepared for you of reward." A door is opened for him at his head toward the Fire, and it is said to him: "Look at what Allah has turned away from you of punishment." Then it is said to him: "Sleep, with your eye at rest." There is nothing more beloved to him than the establishing of the Hour.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"When the believer is placed in his grave, the earth says to him: 'If you were beloved to me while you were upon my back, then how much more so now that you are in my belly. I will show you what I will do with you.' Then his grave is widened for him as far as his sight can reach."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"When the disbeliever is placed in a grave, Munkar and Nakir come to him and make him sit up, and they say to him: 'Who is your Lord?' He says: 'I do not know.' They say: 'May you not have known!' Then they strike him with a blow, and he turns to ashes. Then he is returned and made to sit, and it is said to him: 'What do you say about this man?' He says: 'What man?' They say: 'Muhammad (ﷺ).' He says: 'People say he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Then they strike him with a blow, and he turns to ashes."

This is a well-known, widely transmitted hadith, which a group of the memorizers of hadith (huffaz) have authenticated. We know of no imam of hadith who criticized it. Rather, they narrated it in their books and received it with acceptance, and made it a foundation among the principles of the religion concerning the punishment of the grave and its bliss, the questioning by Munkar and Nakir, the taking of souls, their ascent before Allah, and their return to the grave. As for the statement of Abu Muhammad (Ibn Hazm) that only Zadhan narrated it and that this was an error on his part: in fact, others narrated it from al-Bara' besides Zadhan. It was narrated from him also by 'Adi ibn Thabit, Mujahid ibn Jabr, Muhammad ibn 'Uqbah and others. al-Daraqutni collected its routes in a separate work. Zadhan is among the trustworthy narrators; he narrated from senior Companions such as 'Umar and others, and Muslim included him in his Sahih. Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "Trustworthy (thiqah)." Ḥumayd ibn Hilal was asked about him and said: "He is trustworthy; do not ask about the likes of these." Ibn 'Adi said: "His narrations are acceptable when he narrates from a trustworthy source."

As for the claim that al-Minhal ibn 'Amr alone narrated this addition, namely the words "then his soul is returned to his body," and his weakening of it: al-Minhal is one of the trustworthy and upright narrators. Ibn Ma'in said: "al-Minhal is trustworthy." al-'Ijli said: "Kufan, trustworthy." The worst thing said about him is that he was heard to be in a house where singing was heard, and this does not discredit his narration or justify rejecting his hadith. Ibn Hazm's weakening of him is nothing, for he mentioned no reason for weakening him except his sole narration of the words "his soul is returned to his body." We have already shown that he did not narrate it alone, for others narrated it too.

He also narrated what is more explicit than these, or similar to them, such as: "His soul is returned to him," and: "He goes to the grave and sits up straight," and: "They make him sit," and: "He sits up in his grave." All of these are ṣaḥīḥ (sound) hadiths with no flaw in them. Someone else gave a defect for it, saying that Zadhan did not hear it from al-Bara'. This defect is invalid, for Abu 'Awanah al-Isfara'ini narrated it in his Sahih with an isnad, saying: "From Abu 'Amr Zadhan al-Kindi, who said: 'I heard al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.'" The hafiz Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Mandah said: "This isnad is well-known; a group of them narrated it from al-Bara'."

Even if we set aside the hadith of al-Bara', the other sound hadiths are explicit in this, such as the hadith of Ibn Abi Dhi'b from Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Ata' from Sa'id ibn Yasar from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, the dying person is attended by the angels. If the man is righteous, [the angels] say: 'Come out, O good soul that was in a good body. Come out praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest, sweet fragrance and a Lord who is not angry.' They keep saying this until it comes out. Then it is raised up to heaven, and permission is sought for it, and it is asked: 'Who is this?' They say: 'So-and-so.' They say: 'Welcome to the good soul that was in the body. Enter praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest, sweet fragrance and a Lord who is not angry.' It is told this until it reaches the heaven in which Allah, mighty and majestic, is. If the man is evil, [the angels] say: 'Come out, O evil soul that was in an evil body. Come out reproached, and rejoice in boiling water, dark fluid, and other punishments of their kind.' They keep saying this until it comes out. Then it is raised up to heaven, and permission is sought for it, and it is asked: 'Who is this?' They say: 'So-and-so.' They say: 'No welcome to the evil soul that was in an evil body. Return reproached, for the gates of heaven will not be opened for you.' So it is sent between heaven and earth, and then it goes to the grave. The righteous man sits up in his grave, without fear or hindrance. Then it is said to him: 'What did you used to say about Islam? What about this man?' He says: 'Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He came to us with clear proofs from Allah, so we believed and affirmed him.'" And he mentioned the rest of the hadith.

The hafiz Abu Nu'aym said: "This hadith is one whose transmitters are agreed upon as trustworthy. al-Bukhari and Muslim agreed that Abu Dhi'b, Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Ata', and Sa'id ibn Yasar are among those whose narrations they accept." (End of quote.) Many have narrated it from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, including great early transmitters such as Ibn Abi Fudayk and 'Abd al-Rahim ibn Ibrahim.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Mandah also used as evidence for the return of the soul to the body the following isnad: He said: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Nisaburi narrated to us; Hammad ibn Qayrat narrated to us; Muhammad ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'igh al-Balkhi, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "One day while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting, he recited this verse: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are stretching out their hands﴾ to the end of the verse." He said: "By the One in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, no soul departs from the world without seeing its place in Paradise or the Fire." Then he said: "At that moment, two rows of angels stand before him, filling what is between the two horizons, their faces like the sun. He looks at them, and we see none but them, though if you think they are looking at you, they are with each of them shrouds and embalming spices. If he is a believer, they give him glad tidings of Paradise and say: 'Come out, O good soul, to the pleasure of Allah and His Paradise. Allah has prepared for you of honor what is better than the world and all that is in it.' They keep giving him glad tidings and surrounding him, for they are gentler and kinder than a mother to her child. Then they draw out his soul from beneath every fingernail and joint. The first dies, then the next, and it becomes easy for them, though you thought it was severe, until it reaches his chin. He said: 'It hates leaving the body more than a child hates leaving the womb, so each angel hastens to take it, each wanting to be the one who seizes it, and the Angel of Death takes it.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you, then to your Lord you will be returned﴾. "He receives it with white shrouds, then embraces it to himself, holding it more tightly than a woman holds her child after giving birth. Then a scent more fragrant than musk wafts from it, and they breathe in its fragrance and rejoice at it, saying: 'Welcome, O good soul and good spirit! O Allah, bless it as a spirit, and the body it came out of.' They ascend with it, and Allah, mighty and majestic, has creatures in the air whose number none knows but Him. A scent more fragrant than musk wafts to them from it, so they bless it and rejoice. The gates of heaven are opened for them, and every angel in every heaven they pass blesses it, until it reaches before the Mighty King, majestic is His majesty. [Allah says:] 'Welcome to the good soul and to the body it came out of!' When the Lord, mighty and majestic, says welcome to something, everything welcomes it, and every constriction leaves it. Then He says to this good soul: 'Enter Paradise, show it its place in Paradise, and present to it what I have prepared for it of honor and bliss. Then take it back to the earth, for I have decreed that from it I created them, into it I will return them, and from it I will bring them out once more.' By the One in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, it hates leaving it more when it leaves the body than it did when it was leaving the body, and it says: 'Where are you taking me, to that body I was in?' They say: 'We are commanded to do this, and you must go back to it.' So they bring it down, after they have finished washing its body and shrouding it, and they place that soul between its body and its shrouds."

This hadith shows that the soul is returned between the body and the shrouds. This return is other than the attachment the soul had to the body in the world, and it is a different kind of return. It is also other than its attachment to the body during sleep, and other than its attachment to the body while it is in its place (in the barzakh). Rather, it is a special return for the purpose of questioning.

Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said: "The sound, widely transmitted (mutawatir) hadiths indicate that the soul returns to the body at the time of questioning. The questioning of the body without a soul is a view held by a group of people, which the majority rejected. Others opposed them and said that the questioning is of the soul without a body. This was said by Ibn Murrah and Ibn Hazm, and both are mistaken. The sound hadiths refute it. Had it been of the soul alone, the grave would have no special connection with the soul."

[Section: The Station of Remembrance]

He said: Then the heart descends to the station of remembrance (tadhakkur), and it is the companion of return (inabah) to God. God the Exalted said: ﴿And none remembers except those who turn back in repentance﴾ [Ghafir: 13].

And He said: ﴿An insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ [Qaf: 8]. And it is among the distinctive qualities of the people of understanding (ulu al-albab), as God the Exalted said: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19].

And He the Exalted said: ﴿And none remembers except the people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

Remembrance (tadhakkur) and reflection (tafakkur) are two stations that yield all kinds of knowledge (ma'arif) and the realities of faith (iman) and excellence (ihsan). The knower (arif) never ceases to return with his reflection to his remembrance, and with his remembrance to his reflection, until the lock of his heart is opened by the permission of the All-Opener, the All-Knowing. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "The people of knowledge have always returned with remembrance to reflection and with reflection to remembrance, and they make hearts speak until they speak."

The author of al-Manazil (Sahib al-Manazil, i.e. al-Harawi al-Ansari) said: "Remembrance is above reflection, because reflection is a seeking (talab), and remembrance is a finding (wujud)."

He means that reflection is the pursuit of ends from their beginnings, as he said: "Reflection is the groping of insight to recover the desired aim."

As for his saying that remembrance is a finding (wujud), it is because it occurs regarding what was already attained through reflection and then was lost from him through forgetting; when he remembers it, he finds it and obtains it.

Remembrance (tadhakkur) is a form of tafa''ul from dhikr (remembrance), which is the opposite of forgetting (nisyan). It is the presence in the heart of the knowledge-image (suratu al-madhkur al-ilmiyyah) of the thing remembered. The pattern tafa''ul was chosen for it because it is attained after a delay and gradual progression, like tabassur (perceiving), tafahhum (understanding), and ta'allum (learning).

Thus the station of remembrance relative to reflection is the station of attaining the sought-after thing after searching for it. For this reason, God's signs, both recited (mat luwwah) and witnessed (mashhudah), are called reminders. As He said of the recited signs: ﴿And We gave Moses the guidance, and We made the Children of Israel inherit the Book, a guidance and a reminder for the people of understanding﴾ [Ghafir: 53].

And He said of the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqah: 48].

And He said of His witnessed signs: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it and adorned it, and it has no rifts? And the earth — We spread it out and placed in it firm mountains and caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair, as an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ [Qaf: 6].

So the insight (tabsirah) is the instrument of sight, and the reminder (tadhkirah) is the instrument of remembrance. He joined them together and made them for the people of repentance, because when the servant turns back to God, he sees the locations of the signs and lessons, and he is guided by them to what they are signs of. Thus aversion is removed by repentance, blindness by insight, and heedlessness by reminder, because insight causes the image of the indicated meaning (madlul) to be present in the heart after his heedlessness of it. Therefore the arrangement of the three stations is the best arrangement, and each of them sustains its companion, strengthens it, and makes it fruitful.

And He the Exalted said, regarding His witnessed signs: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in might, and they ranged through the lands — is there any escape? Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf: 36].

Men are of three kinds: a man whose heart is dead — that is the one who has no heart; this verse is not a reminder for him.

The second: a man who has a living, receptive heart, but who does not listen to the recited signs by which God informs about the witnessed signs, either because they have not reached him, or because they have reached him but his heart is occupied with other things and absent from them. He is absent of heart, not present, so for him too the reminder is not attained despite his receptivity and the existence of his heart.

The third: a man with a living, receptive heart, to whom the signs are recited; he inclines his hearing, gives ear, and brings his heart present, not occupying it with anything other than understanding what he hears. He is a heart that witnesses, giving ear. This is the category that benefits from the recited and witnessed signs.

So the first is like the blind man who does not see. The second is like the seeing man who directs his gaze away from the direction of the thing viewed; both of them do not see it. The third is like the seeing man who has fixed his eyes on the direction of the thing viewed, followed it with his sight, and faced it at a moderate distance, neither too far nor too near; this is the one who sees it.

Glory be to Him who made His speech a healing for what is in the breasts.

The author of al-Manazil said: The structures of remembrance are three: benefiting from admonition (i'tibar bil-'izhah), seeking insight from the lesson (istibsar bil-'ibrah), and attaining the fruit of reflection (zafar bi-thamarat al-fikrah).

Benefiting from admonition: it is that a driving force of fear and hope (qadih al-khawf wal-raja') strikes the heart, so that it moves to action, seeking deliverance from fear and desiring the attainment of what is hoped for.

Admonition (i'zah) is the command and prohibition joined with encouragement and warning.

Admonition is of two kinds: admonition through what is heard, and admonition through what is witnessed. Admonition through what is heard is benefiting from what he hears of guidance and right direction, and the counsels that came through the messengers and what was revealed to them; likewise benefiting from admonition from every adviser and guide in matters of religion and the world.

Admonition through what is witnessed is benefiting from what he sees and witnesses in the world of lessons and the decrees of destiny (ahkam al-qadar), their courses, and the signs of God that show the truthfulness of His messengers.

As for seeking insight from the lesson, it is an increase of insight beyond what it was at the station of reflection, through the power of recollection, because remembrance holds fast the meanings that were attained through reflection on the locations of signs and lessons. He obtains them by reflection, and they are polished and made clear to him by remembrance. Thus resolve grows to proceed in proportion to the strength of insight, because it requires the restriction of attention to what moves the seeking, since seeking is a branch of awareness. Whenever awareness of the beloved grows stronger, the heart's journey toward it intensifies; and whenever reflection is occupied with it, awareness of it, insight into it, and remembrance of it increase.

As for attaining the fruit of reflection, this is a subtle matter.

Reflection has two fruits: the attainment of the sought-after thing completely, to the extent possible, and acting upon its requirement, observing its right. For the heart, during reflection, had been exhausted by its labors in attaining the sought-after thing. When the meanings were attained for it and matured in the heart, and the intellect rested, it returned to remember what it had gathered and surveyed, and it rejoiced and was delighted by it, and in this station it corrected what it had missed in the station of reflection, because it had come close to it in the station of remembrance, which is higher than it. Then it set about the intended fruit, which is acting upon its requirement, observing its right, for righteous deeds are the fruit of beneficial knowledge, which is the fruit of reflection.

If you wish to understand this with a sensible example: the seeker of wealth, as long as he is earnest in his pursuit, is in weariness and fatigue; then when he attains it, he rests from the toil of seeking, returns from the journey of trade, surveys what he has gathered and seen, and in this state corrects what he may have erred in while busy with seeking. When it is sound for him and his gain is secured, he sets about spending the wealth on the beneficial ways intended for it. And God knows best.

(Section)

He said: Benefit from admonition comes only after three things are present: intense need for it, blindness to the faults of the admonisher, and remembrance of promise and threat.

The servant's need for admonition, which is encouragement and warning, intensifies when his return and remembrance have weakened. Otherwise, when his return and remembrance are strong, his need for reminding, encouragement, and warning does not become intense; rather, his need becomes intense for knowledge of the command and prohibition.

Admonition is intended to convey two things: the command and prohibition joined with desire and dread, and the desire and dread themselves. The one who returns in repentance and remembers has intense need for the command and prohibition; the heedless one who turns away has intense need for encouragement and warning; and the arrogant opponent has intense need for debate.

These three were addressed to these three in His saying: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. He stated wisdom without restricting it with the description of goodness, since all of it is good and its goodness is intrinsic. As for admonition, He restricted it with the description of excellence, since not every admonition is good.

Likewise, debate may be in the way that is best, and may be otherwise. This may refer to the state of the debater, his harshness or gentleness, his severity or kindness, so that he is commanded to debate them in the best manner. It may also be a description of what is argued with, namely the proofs and demonstrations, and the words that are the best, clearest, most indicative of the intended meaning, and most effective in reaching the sought goal. The truth is that the verse encompasses both types.

As for what some later scholars have mentioned, that this indicates the types of syllogisms (qiyasat): wisdom is the method of demonstration (burhan), good admonition is the method of rhetoric (khitabah), and debate in the way that is best is the method of dialectic (jadal). The first is by presenting demonstrative premises to one who will accept only demonstration and yield only to it, and these are the elite of people. The second is by presenting rhetorical premises that stir desire and dread for one who is content with rhetoric, and these are the masses. The third is by presenting dialectical premises for the opponent who is moved by debate, and these are the adversaries. Thus the revelation of the Qur'an is interpreted according to the rules and terminology of the Greek logicians, and that is definitively false in many respects, which is not the place to mention. This was mentioned only as a digression from the subject of admonition, and that the one who returns and remembers does not have as intense a need for it as the heedless, turning-away person does. For the heedless one has an extremely intense need for admonition so that he may remember what he has forgotten and thereby benefit from remembrance.

As for blindness to the faults of the admonisher: when one is occupied with it, he is deprived of benefit from the admonition, because human souls are naturally disposed not to benefit from the speech of one who does not act by it and does not benefit from it himself. This is like one whom a physician prescribes a medicine for an illness that the physician himself has, while the physician ignores it and pays it no attention. Rather, that physician is in a better condition in their view than this admonisher who contradicts what he preaches, because another medicine may serve in his stead, or he may see in himself the strength to forgo treatment, or he may rely on the body's natural healing, and other such things; whereas what this admonisher preaches is a specific path to salvation, which no other can replace, and it is indispensable. Because of this aversion, Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿And I do not want to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from﴾ [Hud: 88].

And one of the early generation (salaf) said: If you want your command and prohibition to be accepted, then when you command something, be the first to do it, and when you forbid something, be the first to refrain from it. And it has been said:

O you who teach others, why did the teaching not begin with yourself?
You prescribe the medicine for the ill with wasting disease, yet from that wasting you yourself are sick.
Do not forbid a trait while you practice its like; it is a shame upon you when you commit a blameworthy act.
Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error; when it refrains from it, then you are wise.
Then what you say will be accepted and followed, and teaching from you will benefit.

Thus blindness to the faults of the admonisher is one of the conditions for the full benefit of his admonition.

As for remembrance of promise and threat: it necessitates fear of Him and caution against Him, and admonition benefits only one who believes in it, fears it, and hopes for it. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾ [Hud: 103]. And He said: ﴿The one who fears will remember﴾ [al-A'la: 10]. And He said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]. And more explicit than that is His saying: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45]. Thus belief in the promise and the threat, and remembrance of it, is a condition for benefiting from admonitions, signs, and lessons, and its attainment is impossible without it.

He said: And lessons are sought for insight only through three things: the life of the intellect, knowledge of the days (of God, i.e. the events of history), and freedom from ulterior aims.

The true distinction, the seeing and realization of lesson-taking (ʿibrah), comes through the life of the intellect. ʿIbrah is iʿtibar (reflection, drawing a lesson), and its reality is passing over (ʿubur) from the ruling on one thing to the ruling on its like. So when someone sees that a person has been struck by affliction and trial because of a sin he committed, he knows that the ruling for whoever commits that sin is like his ruling.

The life of the intellect is soundness of perception, strength and excellence of understanding, and the realization of benefit from a thing and harm from it. It is a light that Allah singles out for whom He wills of His creation. According to the degree of people's strength or weakness in that light, and its presence or absence in them, their minds, understandings and perceptions differ. Its relation to the heart is like the relation of seeing light to the eye.

Among the experiments of the wayfarers (al-salikin) that they tested and found to be correct is that whoever persistently recites "Yā Ḥayyu, yā Qayyūm, lā ilāha illā anta" (O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting, there is no god but You) gains from it the life of the heart and intellect.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul, was extremely devoted to this recitation. He once said to me: "These two Names, al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm, have a great effect on the life of the heart." He used to indicate that they are the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam). I also heard him say: "Whoever perseveres in saying forty times each day, between the Sunnah of Fajr and the Fajr prayer, 'Yā Ḥayyu, yā Qayyūm, lā ilāha illā anta, bi-raḥmatika astaghīth' (O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting, there is no god but You; by Your mercy I seek help), will attain the life of the heart, and his heart will not die."

Whoever knows the servitude (ʿubūdiyyāt) associated with the Most Beautiful Names and supplication by them, and the secret of their connection with creation and command, and with the servant's needs and requirements, will recognize this and realize it. For every request is asked by means of what is suitable to it. So reflect on the supplications of the Qur'an and the Prophetic hadiths, and you will find them to be so.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 40, verse 19:

He combined the glances (al-lahazat) and the passing thoughts (al-khatarat) in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal.﴾

(Benefit)

Imam Ahmad said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ "It is the man who is among a people when a woman passes by him, and he steals a glance at her with his eyes."

The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the sudden glance (nazrat al-fajah), and he said: "Turn your gaze away from her."

(Benefit)

Many grammarians forbade saying "al-ba'd" (some) and "al-kull" (all), because these two are nouns that are only used in the construct state (as the first term of an idafa).

It occurs in the speech of al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) and others that "al-ba'd" is a substitute (badal) for "al-kull."

Abu 'Ubayda permitted that it could carry the meaning of "al-kull," just as he permitted this for "al-akthar" (most). The first, as in His saying: ﴿Some of what He promises you will befall you﴾

and the second, as in His saying: ﴿And most of them are liars﴾

He has no proof in this, because His saying: ﴿Some of what He promises you﴾ is from the discourse of gentleness and soft speech.

As for ﴿And most of them are liars﴾, it is not impossible that among them are those who speak the truth in many of their statements.

Having understood this, a group said that "al-ba'd" is applied to the small part, the large part, and the equal part.

In this there is room for scrutiny, since applying the term "some of ten" to nine requires transmission and established usage.

It appears that it is close to "al-ba'd" in meaning, just as it is close to it in wording.

Yet in the custom of the language and of discourse, when one says, "Take some of this heap," he does not mean that he should take all of it except a handful; nor does one say to someone who comes to you on all the days of the month, "He came on some of the days of the month," meaning one day only.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 40, verses 32–33:

Mujahid said: "Fārrīn (fleeing) means unable to escape (ghayr mu'jizīn)."

Al-Dahhak said: When they hear the roaring (zafīr) of the Fire, they flee in panic, but they do not come to any direction (qutr) of the regions except that they find the angels arranged in rows, so they return to the place where they were. This is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And the angel will be upon its edges﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17].

And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O company of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through. You will not pass except with authority.﴾ [al-Rahman: 33]

This view is the more apparent, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 40, verses 36–37:

The people of Kufa read «وَصُدَّ» (wa-ṣuddda, "and were turned away") in the passive voice, taking it as parallel to «زُيِّنَ» (zuyyina, "was made attractive"). The rest of the reciters read «وَصَدَّ» (wa-ṣadda) with a fatha on the ṣād, and this reading allows two meanings.

The first: he turned away, in which case the verb is intransitive (lāzim).

The second: he barred and prevented others, in which case the verb is transitive (muta'addī). The two readings are like two verses that do not contradict each other.

As for hardening the heart (al-shadd 'alā al-qalb), it appears in the words of Allah the Exalted: {Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment." He said, "The supplication of you two has been answered, so remain steadfast..."} (10:88–89).

So this hardening of the heart is the same as turning away and preventing.

For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means: prevent it. The meaning is: make it hard and seal it, so that it will not soften and will not open up to faith."

This agrees with what is in the Torah: Allah the Exalted said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh, for I will harden his heart, so that he will not believe until I show My signs and wonders in Egypt."

This hardening and making hard is part of the perfection of the Lord's justice (ʿadl) toward His enemies, for He made it a punishment for them because of their disbelief and turning away, just as He punishes them with calamities. For this reason it is praiseworthy: it is good when it comes from Him, and the most wicked thing when it comes from them, for it is justice and wisdom from Him, and it is injustice and foolishness from them. Thus divine decree (qaḍāʾ) and predestination (qadar) are the acts of a just, wise, self-sufficient, knowing Being who places good and evil in the most fitting places for them. What is decreed and predestined becomes injustice, oppression, and foolishness when it comes from the servant, and it is the act of an ignorant, unjust, foolish one.

(Section)

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways, the ways to the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses"﴾

This indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, used to say: "My God is in the heaven," while Pharaoh thought he was lying. If anyone argues against us about what we have already presented...

He also said: If it were so, it would resemble created things, because whatever is encompassed by places and contained by them is created. Something that is not bound and has no meaning... because He, the Exalted, "there is nothing like unto Him" (42:11) among His creation, and He is not compared with anything of His creatures, nor is He grasped by analogy, nor is He measured with people. He existed before places and will exist after them. There is no god but He, the Creator of all things, with no partner. The Muslims and every person of intellect agree that no existing thing can be conceived except in some place, and that what is not in a place is nonexistent. It is established by reason and proven by evidence that He existed in eternity without a place, and He is not nonexistent. How then can He be compared with anything of His creation, or be likened or assimilated to them? Exalted is Allah above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

If someone says: When we describe our Lord, the Exalted, as having existed in eternity without a place, and then He created places so that He became in a place, this entails our admitting change and transition, since He departed from His attribute in eternity and became in one place rather than another.

It is said to him: Likewise, you claim that He existed without a place and then became in every place. You have thereby transferred His attribute from existing without a place to an attribute of existing in every place. So, according to you, the worshipped has changed and moved from no-place to every place. If he says: He existed in eternity in every place, just as He is now, then he has made places and things co-existent with Him in His eternity, and this is corrupt.

If he says: Is it permissible in your view that He who had no place in eternity moves to a place?

It is said to him: As for movement and change of state, there is no way to apply that to Him, because His existence in eternity does not require a place, and likewise His movement does not require a place. This is not like creation, because the existence of what exists requires "a place" for creatures, and their movement requires a place, and they become moving from one place to another, whereas Allah the Exalted is not like that. . . But we say: He "istawā" (rose over/settled) from no-place to a place, and we do not say "He moved," even though the meaning is the same in both. Just as we say "He has a throne" and do not say "He has a seat," and we say "He is the Wise" and do not say "He is the Intelligent," and we say "the Intimate friend (khalīl) of Abraham" and do not say "the close companion (ṣadīq) of Abraham," even though the meaning is the same. This is because we do not name Him, describe Him, or apply to Him except what He named Himself with, as has been stated before. We also do not reject what He described Himself with, for that would be rejecting the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ (89:22).

His coming is not a motion, nor a removal, nor a transition, because these occur only when the one who comes is a body or a substance. Since it is established that He is not a body, nor a substance, nor an accident, it does not follow that His coming is a motion or a transfer. If you consider this by their saying, "his resurrection came upon so-and-so," "death came to him," "illness came to him," and similar expressions, for what is present and descends upon him is not a "coming" in the physical sense, it would become clear to you. And with Allah is protection and success.

If someone says: He cannot be "istawā" over a place except joined with a how (kayf), it is said to him: "istiwā'" may be obligatory while the "how" (taknīf, specifying a modality) is removed. Removing the "how" does not require removing the "istiwā'." If this were required, then the "how" would have been required in eternity, since He would not be existing in a place or joined to a modality. If he says that He existed without a place and was not joined to a modality, and we have understood and perceived by our senses that we have spirits in our bodies, and we do not know the modality of that, our ignorance of the modality of spirits does not require that we have no spirits. Likewise our ignorance of His modality on His throne does not require that He is not on His throne.

It has been narrated from Abu Razin al-'Uqaili who said:

"I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, where was our Lord, blessed and exalted, before He created the heavens and the earth?' He said, 'He was in 'amā', with nothing above Him, and nothing below Him, and He created the Throne upon the water.'"

Abu al-Qasim said: "'Amā'" (with a long mad) is a cloud, and "'amá" (with a short qaṣr) is darkness. The hadith has been narrated with both the long and the short forms. Whoever narrates it with the long form, its meaning according to him is: He was in a cloud, with what is below it and above it being air, and the pronoun refers to 'amā'. Whoever narrates it with the short form, its meaning according to him is: He was in a state of being "hidden" from His creation, because whoever is blinded from something is darkened concerning it.

Sunayd narrated with his chain from Mujahid, who said: "Between the Throne and the angels there are seventy veils, some of light and some of darkness." Sunayd also narrated with his chain from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The distance between the heaven and the earth is a five-hundred-year journey, and between each heaven and the next is a five-hundred-year journey, and between the seventh heaven and the Kursi is a five-hundred-year journey, and between the Kursi and the water is a five-hundred-year journey, and the Throne is upon the water, and Allah, glory be to Him, is above the Throne, and He knows your deeds."

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, also said: "He is above the Throne, and nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him." Abu al-Qasim said: He means "above the Throne," because the Throne is the last of the created things, and there is nothing above it that is created, and Allah the Exalted is above the created things without modality, without contact. I know of no elevated (marfūʿ) hadith on this subject except the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umayra from al-Ahnaf from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at a cloud and said: "What do you call this?" They said: "The cloud (saḥāb)." He said: "And the rain-cloud (muzn)." They said: "And the rain-cloud." He said: "And the 'anān (cloud-layer)." They said: "And the 'anān." He said: "How far do you think there is between you and the sky?" They said: "We do not know." He said: "Between you and it is either one, or two, or seventy-three years, and the sky above it is likewise, and between them is the same distance," until he counted seven heavens. "Then above the seventh heaven is a sea, its top and bottom as far apart as between one heaven and another. Then above that are eight mountain goats, between their hooves and knees is as far as between one heaven and another. On their backs is the Throne, between its bottom and top is as far as between one heaven and another. Then Allah the Exalted is above that."

This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and sound), related by Abu Dawud.
